Trying to Conceive

How to Use Ovulation Tests and Read the Results

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

To use an ovulation test, dip the strip in urine between late morning and early afternoon, starting a few days before you expect to ovulate, and read it as positive when the test line is as dark as or darker than the control line. That positive means your LH surge has started and ovulation is likely within about 24 to 36 hours. The details matter, though: the day you start, the time you test, and how you judge the lines can all decide whether you catch your surge or miss it.

What an ovulation test actually measures

An ovulation test measures luteinizing hormone, usually shortened to LH, in your urine. Your body makes a small amount of LH all cycle long, then releases a sharp surge that tells an ovary to release an egg. That surge is the signal the test is built to catch, and ovulation usually follows it by roughly 24 to 36 hours. This is why the kits are sometimes called ovulation predictor kits: they predict that ovulation is likely close rather than confirming it happened. Knowing the surge has started gives you a short window to plan sex or insemination while the chance of conception is at its highest.

Most kits come in one of three forms. Inexpensive paper strips are dipped into a cup of urine and are the cheapest way to test often. Midstream sticks look like pregnancy tests and are held in the urine stream. Digital readers use the same chemistry but show a symbol, such as a smiley face or the word peak, instead of lines. All of them detect the same hormone, so the real differences are cost and how easy the result is to read. If you expect to test daily for a week or more each cycle, cheap strips usually make the most sense, with a digital reader as a backup if judging lines frustrates you.

When to start testing in your cycle

Start testing a few days before you expect your LH surge, so you cannot miss it. With a fairly regular 28-day cycle, ovulation often happens around day 14, so beginning around day 10 to 12 works well. Count day 1 as the first day of full menstrual flow. If your cycles are shorter, start earlier: with a 24-day cycle, testing from about day 7 or 8 is reasonable. Longer cycles shift everything later, so a 35-day cycle might mean starting around day 17 or 18. A rough rule that works for many people is to begin about 17 days before your next period is due.

Test once a day at first, at roughly the same time. When the test line starts to darken, or you notice fertile signs like slippery cervical mucus, switch to testing twice a day, once around midday and once in the early evening. LH surges can be short, sometimes lasting less than a day, so twice-daily testing near midcycle makes it much harder to miss the peak. If your cycles are irregular, expect to use more strips and give it more patience, and consider tracking a couple of cycles first to learn your usual range. Note your test days and results in BeMama or on paper so the pattern is easy to see.

The best time of day to test

Unlike pregnancy tests, ovulation tests often work better later in the day. For many people the LH surge begins in the morning and takes several hours to show up in urine, so first-morning urine can miss the start of it. Testing between late morning and early afternoon, roughly 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., catches the surge for most people, and an early-evening test makes a good second check. There is no single perfect hour, and some brands say any time of day is fine. Consistency matters more than perfection, so pick a time you can repeat and stick with it from day to day.

Concentration matters too. Try not to urinate for about 2 to 4 hours before testing, and limit big drinks during that window, because very diluted urine can make a real surge look weaker than it is. Then follow your specific kit: dip a strip to the marked line for the stated number of seconds, or hold a midstream stick in the stream, and lay it flat. Read the result within the time printed in the leaflet, often around 5 to 10 minutes. Strips that sit longer can darken as they dry, so a photo taken at the read time is a fairer record than the dried strip itself.

How to read the lines

A standard strip shows two lines: a control line that proves the test worked, and a test line that responds to LH. The rule here is different from a pregnancy test. An ovulation test is positive only when the test line is as dark as, or darker than, the control line. A faint test line is not a weak positive. Because your body always makes some LH, most days of your cycle will show a faint line, and that is completely normal. What you are watching for is the day the test line suddenly matches or beats the control line in darkness.

Comparing shades can feel subjective, especially under bathroom lighting when you are tired. It helps to keep each day's strip, label it with the cycle day, and line them up side by side in daylight. Many people see a clear progression: faint, darker, then unmistakably dark. If judging shades stresses you, a digital reader removes the guesswork by showing a clear symbol when it detects the surge, at a higher cost per test. Once you have a clear positive, you can stop testing for that cycle. The useful information is that the surge has started, and darker lines after that add nothing.

What a positive means, and what it cannot tell you

A positive ovulation test means your fertile window is now. Ovulation usually follows the start of the surge by about 24 to 36 hours, and an egg survives roughly 12 to 24 hours after release, while sperm can live for several days. Practically, that makes the day of your first positive and the next two days your best days for sex or insemination. You do not need to time anything to the hour. If you have already been having sex every day or two through the fertile week, a positive simply confirms you are on track, not that you must act at a specific moment.

An ovulation test cannot prove an egg was actually released. Occasionally the body surges without ovulating, and tracking basal body temperature is a simple complementary way to confirm ovulation after the fact. Conditions like PCOS can keep LH elevated and produce misleading positives, which our PCOS tracking guide covers in detail. An LH strip is also not a reliable pregnancy test, even though the hormones are related. If you test through two or three cycles and never see a positive, or your cycles are very irregular, mention it to a clinician. The same advice applies if you have been trying to conceive for 12 months without success, or for 6 months if you are 35 or older. These patterns have many possible explanations, and they are worth a proper look rather than more months of guessing.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Cycle length and ovulation timing vary, so calendar dates and home fertility signs provide estimates rather than proof. Temperature usually rises after ovulation, cervical mucus may change beforehand, and urine tests detect a hormone surge that suggests ovulation may follow.

Sleep disruption, illness, travel, breastfeeding, hormonal contraception, and irregular cycles can make patterns harder to interpret. Combining observations may provide useful context, but no home method confirms fertility or guarantees pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can place periods, temperatures, cervical mucus, symptoms, and test results on one timeline. Fertile-window dates are educational estimates and must not be used as contraception.

When to seek help

Contact a healthcare professional for persistently absent, very painful, unusually heavy, or highly irregular periods, or when a medical condition may affect fertility.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Fertility Awareness-Based Methods of Family Planning
  • ACOG — Evaluating Infertility

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Ovulation tests detect the LH surge that comes about 24 to 36 hours before ovulation.
  • Start testing around day 10 to 12 of a 28-day cycle, earlier for shorter cycles and later for longer ones.
  • Test between late morning and early afternoon, and limit fluids for a couple of hours beforehand.
  • A test is positive only when the test line is as dark as or darker than the control line; faint lines are normal.
  • Your best days for conception are the day of a positive and the two days after it.

Frequently asked questions

How long after a positive ovulation test do you ovulate?

Ovulation usually happens about 24 to 36 hours after your LH surge begins, so often within a day or so of your first positive test. The egg then survives roughly 12 to 24 hours. That is why the day of the positive and the two days after it are the best days to try.

What time of day should I take an ovulation test?

Late morning to early afternoon works well for most people, because a surge that starts in the morning takes a few hours to reach your urine. First-morning urine can miss it. Limit large drinks and try not to urinate for about two to four hours before testing, and keep your testing time consistent from day to day.

What does a faint line on an ovulation test mean?

A faint test line usually means your LH is at its normal background level and you are not surging yet. Unlike a pregnancy test, a visible line alone does not count as positive. Keep testing daily; the result is positive only when the test line is as dark as or darker than the control line.

Why is my ovulation test always negative?

The most common reasons are starting too late or stopping too early in your cycle, testing with very diluted urine, or missing a short surge between tests. Testing twice a day around midcycle catches most surges. If you see no positive across two or three cycles, or your cycles are very irregular, bring it up with a clinician.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
